questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Asymptote of a Rational Function
questions.problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{14{x}^{3}}{6{x}^{3}+1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{14{x}^{3}}{6{x}^{3}+1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{14{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{6{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{14}{(6+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{14}{6+0} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ is $y=\frac{7}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying When a Rational Function has No Horizontal Asymptote
questions.problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{4{x}^{3}+6}{5x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{4{x}^{3}+6}{5x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{x}+\frac{6}{x})}{(\frac{5x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(4{x}^{2}+\frac{6}{x})}{5} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(4{x}^{2}+0)}{5} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote.

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Limit at Infinity: Infinite Solutions
questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{3}-x}{{x}^{2}-3} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{(x-\frac{1}{x})}{(1-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{x-0}{1-0} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }x \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Limit at Infinity: Infinite Solutions
questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{5}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{8{x}^{6}+5}{2{x}^{5}-7x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{8{x}^{6}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{5}{{x}^{5}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{7x}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(8x+\frac{5}{{x}^{5}})}{(2-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{8x+0}{2-0} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,4x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Asymptote of a Rational Function
questions.problem:
What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ for $x>0$ with $f(x)=\frac{|3-8x|}{4x+1}?$

The horizontal asymptote is $y=$

{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
For large positive values of $x,$ we have $|3-8x|=8x-3.$ Consequently, for $x\to \infty ,$ we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{|3-8x|}{4x+1}={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{8x-3}{4x+1}.
$$

The horizontal asymptote for $x>0$ is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{8x-3}{4x+1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{8x}{x}-\frac{3}{x})}{(\frac{4x}{x}+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(8-\frac{3}{x})}{(4+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =\frac{8-0}{4+0} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$
